Posted May 15, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: This is an extremely important article at a crucial time. Of course, it stands in sharp contrast to events in DEAland.
See
The Ultimate Hypocrisy: " Justice " Thomas, Who Smoked Marijuana At Yale Law School, Writes Supreme Court Opinion Against Medical Cannabis. Drug War Depends Upon Persecution of Sick and Dying.

The fact that appeared the day after the Supreme Court ruling is a coincidence, but events in Canada are moving at their own pace. Other than among the lumpen narks, there is very little opposition to decriminalization remaining in Canada. Even the Canadian Chiefs of Police have come out in favor of it, so this is not as " bold " as it may seem. Of course, some Canadian politicians give the impression that they look to DEAland and not to the Canadian people for guidance on marijuana policies.
See
Ottawa Citizen’s Dan Gardner Says " U.S. Bullies World Into Waging Futile Drug War " --UK Article Demonstrates How This Continues.
and links

Decriminalization in Canada would have a significant effect in the UK as well as DEAland, although the narks would surely lie about Canada, just as they have lied about The Netherlands.

The footnotes are links to important resources. Check them out.)

From the Journal of The Canadian Medical Association
Marijuana: federal smoke clears, a little

May 15, 2001
Fourteen years after narcotics police arrested Terrance Parker (who had discovered that smoking marijuana reduced the frequency of his grand mal seizures), and a year after the Ontario Court of Appeal ruled that Canada's discretionary regulation of the medicinal use of marijuana was " unfettered and unstructured ... [and] not consistent " with the principles of fundamental justice, " (Note #1) our federal government has taken the bold little step of drafting new regulations.

In Canada, even the simple possession of small amounts of marijuana for personal use is a criminal offense, unless you are one of the roughly 40 Canadians who have obtained a special dispensation to use cannabis to relieve the symptoms of cancer, AIDS, multiple sclerosis or epilepsy.
(MarijuanaNews note: At this point it is actually around 200, but the BC Compassion Club alone has almost 1,500 members and a waiting list.)

The program is unduly restrictive. The new regulations promise more transparency in the review of applications to grow or possess medicinal marijuana, a broader definition of medical necessity, and greater latitude for physicians in determining the needs of individual patients.
See
We Are Winning! Canadian Medical Marijuana Program: Politically Very Important, Medically and Scientifically Absurd.

There are no persuasive randomized trials of marijuana therapy for the relief of symptoms such as pain and nausea.
See
People With AIDS Benefit From – Not Harmed by Medical Marijuana in Government Approved Test. Politically Very Important – Medically Pointless.

Such trials are extremely difficult to do. But the ratio of drug effect (however subjective that effect may be) to drug harm is large: there are no reported cases of fatal marijuana overdose. The risks of lung cancer (from the tars in the smoke) or the very weak (and perhaps nonexistent) risk of addiction are mostly irrelevant to patients with terminal disease or severe chronic conditions.
(MarijuanaNews note: That statement may be a subtle dig at Canadian " Addiction Specialists " who oppose medical cannabis, claiming that it is " addictive " – as though doctors never prescribe addictive drugs.)
See
Is marijuana addictive?
and links

About 400 000 Canadians use cannabis for medical reasons.(Note #2)

Professional organizations such as the CMA must move quickly to issue guidelines for physicians who, increasingly, will be asked for advice by their patients.

Health Canada's decision to legitimize the medicinal use of marijuana is a step in the right direction. But a bolder stride is needed. The possession of small quantities for personal use should be decriminalized. The minimal negative health effects of moderate use (Note #3) would be attested to by the estimated 1.5 million Canadians who smoke marijuana for recreational purposes(Note.#2) The real harm is the legal and social fallout. About half of all drug arrests in Canada are for simple possession of small amounts of marijuana: about 31 299 convictions in 1995 alone. (Note #4)
(MarijuanaNews note: The number is now over 50,000 per year. Roughly 4,000 actually result in jail time.)
See also
Canada's Crime Rate Dropped In 1999 For 8th Consecutive Year Without Creating A Police State. But Marijuana Arrests Continue to Climb. Alcohol Related Violence Soars in UK. Lessons for Everyone.

Many lead to jail terms or fines and all result in that indelible social tattoo: a criminal record. This means that for anyone who's ever been caught with a stash in his or her pocket, the question " Have you ever had a criminal conviction? " during a job application or medical school interview can force higher aspirations to go up in a puff of smoke.
See
Ottawa Citizen Practices First Class Journalism
A Brilliantly Insightful Editorial: " Marijuana isn’t just a serious issue. It’s huge. "

The decriminalization of marijuana possession for personal use does not mean making marijuana " legal " or letting it be sold in every schoolyard.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, only legalization can keep it from " being sold in every schoolyard. " Decriminalization is a step in the right direction, but it keeps marijuana in the black market along with hard drugs.) See
Professor Of Medicine At The University Of Toronto Urges Canada To " Go Dutch " At Vancouver Conference On Health, Addictions And Social Justice.

It does mean that possession of small amounts for personal use would become a civil offense, like a traffic violation, not a criminal one. The provisions of Canada's Contraventions Act make this a relatively simple legislative task.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, it would be an " administrative " task. It can be done without an act of parliament, although there is some controversy about that. In any case, under a parliamentary system where one party has an absolute majority as is the case in Ottawa, the government could do this without any difficulty.)

Mr. Justice Minister, let's decriminalize the possession of small amounts of marijuana for personal use. — CMAJ
(MarijuanaNews note: An article in today’s Ottawa Citizen by by Janice Tibbetts reports:
" A spokeswoman for Ms. McLellan said the minister welcomes debate on decriminalization of marijuana but has no immediate plan to drop possession from the Criminal Code.
'It is far too complex to just move ahead without fully understanding what the social, what the legal and what the educational impacts may be,' said Farah Mohammed...
See
Canadian Justice Minister’s Bizarre Non-Response to Ottawa Citizen’s Dan Gardner.
and links

Among other things, the government is awaiting the outcome of the deliberations of the special Senate committee on illegal drugs, which was struck last year….

Tory Senator Pierre Claude Nolin, who has already said marijuana possession has no place in the Criminal Code, said the message to decriminalize has been delivered loud and clear from witnesses who have appeared before the Senate committee so far. "

References

1. R v Parker (31 July 2000). (Ont. C.A.). (accessed 2001 Apr 19).
See also
Canadian Court Says Lack of Provision for Medical Marijuana Violates Fundamental Rights; Gives Parliament 12 Months to Fix Marijuana Prohibition -- Or There Will Be No Marijuana Laws in Canada.

2. Ogborne AC, Smart RG, Adlaf EM. Self-reported medical use of marijuana: a survey of the general population. CMAJ 2000;162(12):1685-6.

3. Hall W. The cannabis policy debate: finding a way forward [editorial]. CMAJ 2000;162(12):1690-2.

4. Single E, Fischer B, Room R, Poulin C, Sawka E, Thompson H, et al. Cannabis control in Canada: options regarding posession. Ottawa: Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse; 1998.
